# Introduction

Madrid's rental market is strongly segmented by location: a flat in Salamanca can easily rent for twice times a comparable property in Puente de Vallecas. This makes absolute price prediction less informative for renters trying to assess whether a listing is good value. The question I want to answer is: given a property's observable features, is it priced *Low*, *Fair*, or *High* relative to its own district?

The approach is a two stage pipeline. First, I train regression models to predict `rent_price` directly. The predicted value is then converted to a price tier using district specific quartile boundaries, these boundaries are computed entirely on the training set, so there is no leakage from the test data. I compare three models: Elastic Net, Random Forest, and XGBoost. All three are tuned using race-ANOVA elimination [@finetune] inside a unified `workflow_set`, which makes the comparison straightforward and reproducible.

# Data

## Overview

The dataset `houses_madrid.csv` contains rental listings scraped from Idealista. After stratified sampling (preserving representation across neighbourhoods), the working dataset has around **9924 properties** and 58 input features before preprocessing. @tbl-vars lists the main variable groups.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-vars
#| tbl-cap: "Variable groups used in modelling."

tibble::tribble(
  ~Group, ~Examples,
  "Size", "sq_mt_built, sq_mt_useful, total_room",
  "Location", "district, floor",
  "Amenities", "has_ac, has_lift, has_parking, ...", 
  "Property type", "house_type_id, is_new_development",
  "Energy", "energy_certificate, heating_type", 
  "Target", "rent_price -> Low / Fair / High"
) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 8, latex_options = "hold_position")
```

The target variable is constructed by grouping properties within each district and labelling those below the 25th percentile as *Low*, above the 75th as *High*, and everything in between as *Fair*.

# Preprocessing and Feature Engineering

## Manual transformations

Before building the models, I need to clean up the raw columns to remove text noise and redundant features. First, I use `stri_trans_general()` from the stringi package [@stringi] to strip accents from all text. This standardizes the Spanish characters and stops encoding errors when the file runs on different computers. Next, I use a regular expression to split the messy `neighborhood_id` column into three clean fields: `barrio`, `avg_m2_price`, and `district`. I also convert Spanish floor descriptions into numbers ($Sotano \rightarrow -1, Bajo \rightarrow 0, Entreplanta \rightarrow 0.5$) so the model can understand building height as a continuous scale. Besides, I merge the two separate `heating` checkboxes into a single factor column with three clear choices: "central", "individual", or "none". Lately, I combined `n_rooms` and `n_bathrooms` into a single variable `total_room`.

To handle the massive price differences between Madrid neighborhoods, I create a location based `target` variable. A fixed price threshold does not work well because a specific rent might buy a luxury apartment in a working class area, but only a small studio in a premium district. To fix this, I **group the data by district and use the local 25th and 75th percentiles** to label each property **.** This creates a clean, ordered category for our **`target`:** Low (bottom 25%), Fair (middle 50%), and High (top 25%) .

For the final modeling, I must prevent data leakage. I delete raw room counts, helper variables, and avg_m2_price (since it contains future market averages that would let the model cheat). While I calculate these percentiles on the whole dataset here for data cleaning, the actual machine learning workflow calculates the quartile boundaries only from the training data. I then map these exact boundaries onto the test data, ensuring a fair validation and reliable results on any computer.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: data-cleaning


remove_accents <- function(x) stri_trans_general(as.character(x), "Latin-ASCII")
clean_data <- raw_data |>
  dplyr::select(where(~ !all(is.na(.x)))) |>
  mutate(across(
    c(title, subtitle, raw_address, street_name, floor, neighborhood_id, energy_certificate),
    ~ remove_accents(.x)
  )) |>
  extract(
    neighborhood_id,
    into = c("barrio", "avg_m2_price", "district"),
    regex = "Neighborhood \\d+: (.+) \\((.+) .+/m2\\) - District \\d+: (.+)",
    convert = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(
    is_exterior = case_when(
      str_detect(floor, "exterior") ~ TRUE,
      str_detect(floor, "interior") ~ FALSE,
      TRUE ~ is_exterior
    ),
    floor_temp = floor |>
      str_replace_all("Semi-sotano", "-0.5") |>
      str_replace_all("Sotano", "-1") |>
      str_replace_all("Bajo", "0") |>
      str_replace_all("Entreplanta", "0.5"),
    floor = parse_number(floor_temp),
    floor = replace_na(floor, 0),
    energy_certificate = case_when(
      energy_certificate %in% c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G") ~ energy_certificate,
      TRUE ~ "unknown"
    ),
    energy_certificate = factor(energy_certificate,
      levels = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "unknown"),
      ordered = TRUE
    ),
    heating_type = case_when(
      has_central_heating == TRUE ~ "central",
      has_individual_heating == TRUE ~ "individual",
      TRUE ~ "none"
    ),
    total_room = n_bathrooms + n_rooms
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(rent_price), rent_price > 0) |>
  group_by(district) |>
  mutate(
    med = median(rent_price, na.rm = TRUE),
    q25 = quantile(rent_price, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q75 = quantile(rent_price, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    target = case_when(
      rent_price < q25 ~ "Low",
      rent_price > q75 ~ "High",
      TRUE ~ "Fair"
    ),
    target = factor(target, levels = c("Low", "Fair", "High"))
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    across(where(is.character), as.factor),
    across(where(is.logical), as.factor)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(-c(
    id, floor_temp, "...1", avg_m2_price, buy_price, buy_price_by_area,
    street_name, street_number, operation, subtitle, raw_address, title,
    is_floor_under, is_rent_price_known, is_buy_price_known,
    med, q25, q75, has_central_heating, has_individual_heating,
    n_bathrooms, n_rooms
  ))
```

## Why area-relative thresholds?

```{r}
#| label: fig-district-box
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 6.5

clean_data |>
  mutate(district = fct_reorder(district, rent_price, median)) |>
  ggplot(aes(rent_price, district)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.4, outlier.alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Monthly Rent (EUR)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

@fig-district-box confirms the segmentation: medians range from around 700 EUR in the cheapest districts to over 1500 EUR in the most expensive. A property at 900 EUR would be overpriced in Villaverde but underpriced in Chamberi. Using district specific thresholds makes the classification much more meaningful.

## Preprocessing recipe

```{r}
#| label: split
#| cache: true
#| dependson: "data-load"

set.seed(20260513)
data_split <- initial_split(clean_data, prop = 0.8, strata = target)
train_data <- training(data_split)
test_data <- testing(data_split)
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 10, strata = target)

district_ref <- train_data |>
  group_by(district) |>
  summarise(
    q25 = quantile(rent_price, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q75 = quantile(rent_price, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: recipe
#| echo: true
#| cache: true
#| dependson: split

rec_linear <- recipe(rent_price ~ ., data = train_data) |>
  step_rm(target) |>
  step_filter_missing(all_predictors(), threshold = 0.5) |>
  step_impute_knn(all_numeric_predictors(), neighbors = 5) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_factor()) |>
  step_lencode_mixed(barrio, outcome = vars(rent_price)) |> 
  step_ns(floor, deg_free = 3) |> 
  step_nzv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_interact(terms = ~ starts_with("floor"):starts_with("has_lift")) |> 
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_pls(all_numeric_predictors(), outcome = "rent_price", num_comp = 3)

rec_tree <- recipe(rent_price ~ ., data = train_data) |>
  step_rm(target) |>
  step_filter_missing(all_predictors(), threshold = 0.5) |>
  step_impute_knn(all_numeric_predictors(), neighbors = 5) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_factor()) |>
  step_lencode_mixed(barrio, outcome = vars(rent_price)) |> 
  step_nzv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), one_hot = TRUE) |> 
  step_zv(all_predictors())
```

`step_filter_missing` drops columns with more than 50% missing values. KNN imputation (`k = 5`) for numeric variables because it is more better than mean imputation; mode is used for factors. Yeo-Johnson reduces skewness in the numeric predictors. 

Parametric structures were fed into a specialized preprocessing pipeline featuring Mixed-Effect Target Encoding `step_lencode_mixed()` to extract local signals from high-cardinality neighborhood vectors `barrio` without degrees of freedom expansion. Multi-collinearity among real estate geometry variables was resolved using a supervised Partial Least Squares Regression `step_pls` dimensional compression.

# Modeling and Validation

## Model specifications

The Elastic Net serves as a linear baseline. Random Forest and XGBoost are both included because they handle non-linearities and interactions between features that a linear model cannot capture. The number of trees is fixed (200 for RF, 250 for XGBoost) to keep tuning tractable, and the most impactful hyperparameters are searched instead.

## Race-ANOVA tuning with workflow_set

`workflow_set` [@workflowsets] lets me define two different recipes for different models at once and tune them together. `tune_race_anova` [@finetune] is an efficient alternative to evaluating all 20 grid configurations on all 10 folds: after each resample it eliminates distinguishable parameters from the current set, stopping early.

```{r}
#| label: tuning
#| cache: true
#| dependson: "recipe"
#| output: false

lm_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) |>
  set_engine("glmnet")

rf_spec <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = 200) |>
  set_engine("ranger", num.threads = 1, importance = "impurity") |>
  set_mode("regression")

xgb_spec <- boost_tree(
  trees = 250, tree_depth = tune(), learn_rate = tune(), min_n = tune()
) |>
  set_engine("xgboost", nthread = 1) |>
  set_mode("regression")

model_set <- workflow_set(
  preproc = list(linear_pipe = rec_linear, tree_pipe = rec_tree),
  models  = list(elastic_net = lm_spec, random_forest = rf_spec, xgboost = xgb_spec),
  cross = TRUE
) |> 
  filter(!(wflow_id %in% c("linear_pipe_random_forest", "linear_pipe_xgboost")))

plan(multisession, workers = 4)
options(future.globals.maxSize = 4000 * 1024^2)

set.seed(20260513)
all_tune_results <- model_set |>
  workflow_map(
    fn        = "tune_race_anova",
    resamples = cv_folds,
    grid      = 20,
    metrics   = metric_set(rmse, rsq),
    control   = control_race(verbose_elim = FALSE, save_pred = FALSE)
  )

plan(sequential)
```

```{r}
#| label: finalise
#| cache: true
#| dependson: "tuning"

best_summary <- rank_results(all_tune_results, rank_metric = "rmse", select_best = TRUE)

best_wflow_id <- best_summary$wflow_id[1]

best_wflow <- model_set |> 
  extract_workflow(best_wflow_id)

best_params <- all_tune_results |>
  extract_workflow_set_result(best_wflow_id) |>
  select_best(metric = "rmse")

final_fit <- best_wflow |>
  finalize_workflow(best_params) |>
  last_fit(split = data_split)

collect_metrics(final_fit)

prediction_analysis <- final_fit |>
  collect_predictions() |>
  bind_cols(test_data |> dplyr::select(district,barrio,target)) |>
  left_join(district_ref, by = "district") |>
  mutate(
    pred_price = .pred,
    pred_class = case_when(
      pred_price < q25 ~ "Low",
      pred_price > q75 ~ "High",
      TRUE ~ "Fair"
    ),
    pred_class = factor(pred_class, levels = c("Low", "Fair", "High")),
    price_diff = rent_price - pred_price
  )
```

# Results

## Model comparison

```{r}
#| label: fig-autoplot
#| fig-cap: "CV RMSE for all three models across hyperparameter configurations retained by race-ANOVA. Lower is better."
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 6

autoplot(all_tune_results, metric = "rmse") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  labs(y = "CV RMSE (EUR)", x = "Configuration (race-ANOVA retained)")
```

As @fig-autoplot shows, Random Forest edges out XGBoost a little in cross validated RMSE, but both tree models outperform the Elastic Net.

## Test-set performance

```{r}
#| label: tbl-test-metrics
#| tbl-cap: "Final testset metrics for the selected model."

cm <- conf_mat(prediction_analysis, truth = target, estimate = pred_class)

final_metrics <- collect_metrics(final_fit) |>
  dplyr::select(.metric, .estimate) |>
  bind_rows(tibble(
    .metric = "class_accuracy",
    .estimate = accuracy(prediction_analysis,
      truth = target,
      estimate = pred_class
    )$.estimate
  )) |>
  mutate(
    Metric = c("RMSE", "R squared", "Accuracy"),
    Value  = round(.estimate, 3)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(Metric, Value)

kable(final_metrics, booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9, latex_options = "hold_position")
```

The final Random Forest model explains around 82.8\% of rent variance, with test RMSE of about 249 EUR. On classification, accuracy is 75.8\%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-confmat
#| fig-cap: "Confusion matrix heatmap for the three-class price tier classification."
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 3.4

autoplot(cm, type = "heatmap") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The confusion matrix (@fig-confmat) shows that most errors are between classes: Low predicted as Fair, or Fair as High. Very few properties are misclassified across the full span (Low predicted as High). This is reassuring: the continuous regression output means the model still captures relative price ordering.

## Predicted vs. actual and residuals

```{r}
#| label: fig-pred-actual
#| fig-cap: "Left: predicted vs. actual rent with identity line (dashed). Right: residuals vs. actual rent with a loess smoother."
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-width: 6.5

p1 <- ggplot(prediction_analysis, aes(pred_price, rent_price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Predicted (EUR)", y = "Actual (EUR)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

p2 <- ggplot(prediction_analysis, aes(rent_price, price_diff)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.7, colour = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Actual Rent (EUR)", y = "Residual (EUR)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

p1+p2
```

Predictions track actual values well up to around 2000 EUR (@fig-pred-actual, left). The residual plot reveals the model underestimates luxury properties. This is expected: higher quality rentals depend on features like renovation quality and building prestige that are not in the data.

## Feature importance

```{r}
#| label: fig-vip
#| fig-cap: "Top 15 predictors by gain importance for the final model."
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 5.5

final_fit |>
  extract_fit_parsnip() |>
  vip::vip(num_features = 15, aesthetics = list(fill = "midnightblue", alpha = 0.8)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  labs(x = "Importance", y = NULL)
```

The `squre_meter_built` feature ranks first by a large margin (@fig-vip). `Barrio` is also important to tenant which is related to the safety of the area. Lift availability (`has_lift`) comes fourth, which likely acts as a proxy for building age and general quality. `Floor` level, `parking` and several district indicators follow, confirming that both vertical position and location matter.

Also we can that north areas have more higher ranks than other areas. That maybe related with tenants' working accessibilities.

## District level error

```{r}
#| label: tbl-district
#| tbl-cap: "Testset RMSE by district (top 8)."

prediction_analysis |>
  group_by(district) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    RMSE = round(sqrt(mean(price_diff^2, na.rm = TRUE)), 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n >= 30) |>
  arrange(desc(RMSE)) |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9, latex_options = "hold_position")
```

Errors are higher in central and upmarket districts (@tbl-district), which tend to have more transportation convenience and affluent members.

# Conclusions

Framing the rent prediction problem as a district relative classification turns out to work well. By first predicting a continuous rent and then converting it using locally calibrated thresholds, the pipeline separates the regression task from the interpretation layer. The final Random Forest model achieves 75.8\% classification accuracy, well above the 51% majority baseline and errors are mostly between adjacent tiers rather than across the full span.
